name: 湯島 天神下 炭屋
address_ja: 〒113-0034 東京都文京区湯島3-32-14 三王湯島ビル 1F
cuisine: Charcoal 原始焼き izakaya below Yushima Tenjin: bincho charcoal stood on end, skewers grilled upright in front of you, the house 湯島のさば (Yushima mackerel) the thing to order — lunch grilled-fish teishoku with free rice and miso refills around ¥1,000–2,000, dinner with sake ¥5,000–8,000
neighborhood: Yushima 3-chōme, one block from Yushima Tenmangū — 1–2 min from Yushima Station exit 3 (Tokyo Metro Chiyoda line), 6–7 min from JR Okachimachi south exit (Yamanote / Keihin-Tōhoku)
hours_raw: 月・火・水・木・金 11:30～14:30（L.O.14:00）／17:30～22:00（L.O.21:30）　土曜・日曜・祝日 定休　※仕込み状況によって閉店時間が異なる可能性がございます（自社サイトは昼をL.O.13:30と表記）
gf_detail: No gluten-free claim anywhere on the shop's site or its Tabelog page, and nothing suggests wheat-free handling. The grilling itself is the promising part — 原始焼き is salt-and-charcoal, skewers stood upright over bincho, so a plain shio-grilled fish is inherently close to gluten-free. What defeats it as written is everything around it: the teishoku comes with miso soup (miso is wheat- or barley-fermented unless stated otherwise), the izakaya card runs to simmered and glazed dishes built on ordinary wheat soy sauce, and there is no published allergen sheet. A celiac would have to ask in Japanese, order shio-only, and decline the tsuyu and the soup.
vegan_detail: A fish-first Japanese kitchen — the concept sentence is literally grilled mackerel and sake, the site lists 旬の魚介・厳選肉・新鮮野菜 grilled on the same charcoal, and 焼きさば寿司 and mackerel bentō are the takeaway line. Vegetables are skewered and grilled beside the fish, the house dashi is undisclosed, and there is no vegan set. Treat it as a no.

roles: owner-operated Japanese restaurant (日本料理店), opened December 2018
chef_bio.origin: Yushima 3-chōme, Bunkyō-ku — a ground-floor unit of the Sannō Yushima Building at the foot of the Yushima Tenmangū approach
chef_bio.background: The shop does not publish a chef name, and honesty is better than a guess here: neither the official site, the Tabelog listing nor the linked Facebook and Instagram accounts name the owner or the grill cook. What the shop does put its name to is a method. 原始焼き — 'primitive grilling' — means standing bincho charcoal on end and setting skewered ingredients upright beside it rather than laying them on a grate, so the food cooks in radiant heat and its fat is sealed in rather than dripped away. They apply it to a signature they call 湯島のさば, a fatty mackerel with crisp skin and soft flesh, and extend it to seasonal seafood, selected meat and vegetables grilled in front of the customer at the counter. The room is small — 18 seats, 8 of them counter — and the counter is explicitly pitched at the solo drinker; the site carries a page headed 一人呑みのすゝめ, in praise of drinking alone. Alongside the restaurant they run a takeaway and short-radius delivery line of grilled-mackerel bentō and 焼きさば寿司 aimed at nearby offices, made to order and slow-grilled, with pre-ordering advised.
chef_bio.philosophy: One method done properly: upright bincho charcoal, a single signature fish, and regional sake chosen to sit behind it rather than in front of it.
chef_bio.specialty: 湯島のさば — 原始焼き grilled mackerel; grilled-fish teishoku at lunch; 焼きさば寿司 and mackerel bentō to take away.
chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site (yushimatenjinshita-sumiya.com) gives the address 〒113-0034 東京都文京区湯島3丁目32-14 三王湯島ビル1F, the phone 03-6284-2819, hours 11:30～14:00（L.O.13:30）/17:30～22:00（L.O.21:30）with Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays closed, the 原始焼き explanation, the 湯島のさば signature, the free rice and miso refills at lunch, and the takeaway/delivery line. Tabelog 13229993 corroborates the address and phone, dates the opening to December 2018, and adds 18 seats (8 counter), lunch to 14:30 (L.O.14:00), cards at dinner only, a ¥650 otōshi charge on à-la-carte orders, and a ¥5,000–5,999 dinner / ¥1,000–1,999 lunch budget. Neither source names a chef and neither mentions allergens.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No allergen page and no gluten-free claim. Fish, meat and vegetables all pass over the same bincho charcoal at the same counter, so any glazed or floured item that goes through contaminates the shared grill.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese izakaya seasoning; no gluten-free tamari is named anywhere, so assume wheat soy sauce in every dipping sauce, glaze and simmered dish. The lunch teishoku's miso soup is also unspecified — 麦味噌 (barley miso) cannot be ruled out.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetables are skewered and grilled beside mackerel and meat on the same charcoal; the house dashi is undisclosed and the shop's whole identity is fish.

positives.text: An 8-seat counter facing the grill, explicitly pitched at solo diners, so you can watch exactly how your fish is cooked and speak directly to the cook — the best position from which to ask about seasoning.
Reservations accepted and cards taken at dinner (VISA/Master/JCB/AMEX/Diners), which makes arranging a dietary conversation in advance realistic.

cultural_comfort.note: A small Japanese-language neighbourhood restaurant rather than a tourist room: 18 seats, no English menu advertised, and smoking is separated rather than banned (there is a smoking room). It is easy to reach — 93 m from Yushima Station — takes phone reservations, and the counter is designed for people eating alone, so a solo traveller will not feel out of place. Lunch is the low-pressure entry point: a fixed grilled-fish teishoku with free rice and miso refills, ¥1,000–2,000. Watch for the ¥650 per-person otōshi if you order à la carte in the evening, cards at dinner only, and closure every Saturday, Sunday and public holiday — an easy trap for a weekend visitor.

Tabelog 13229993 and the shop's own site agree on 〒113-0034 東京都文京区湯島3-32-14 三王湯島ビル1F and the phone 03-6284-2819; coordinates replaced with the Tabelog geo (35.707647, 139.769264), which moves the pin roughly 500 m from the neighbourhood-centroid guess. Hours flagged irregular because the two sources disagree on lunch last order (site 13:30, Tabelog 14:00) and the shop itself warns closing time varies with prep. No source publishes a chef name, so chef_bio.chef_name is left null rather than guessed. No allergen or gluten-free information exists anywhere — gf_confidence 'ask' reflects absence of evidence, not a shop that declined.

name: 大黒家天麩羅 本店
cuisine: The 1887 Asakusa tendon house on Denbōin-dōri — prawns fried in pure sesame oil and dunked whole in a near-black sweet-salty tare until the batter goes soft and soaks the rice; tendon ¥2,300–2,700, teishoku ¥2,900, cash only, expect a queue
neighborhood: Asakusa 1-chōme on Denbōin-dōri, a two-minute walk inside Kaminarimon — 308 m from Asakusa Station (Tokyo Metro Ginza line exit 1, Toei Asakusa line exit A4, Tobu Skytree line main exit, Tsukuba Express)
hours_raw: 11:00 - 20:00（月・火・水・木・金・土・日）　※営業時間・定休日は変更となる場合がございますので、ご来店前に店舗にご確認ください
gf_detail: Structurally impossible, and it is worth being blunt about why. The entire menu is wheat batter deep-fried in one shared sesame-oil kettle — that is the shop's single product. The tare the tempura is dunked in is a soy-sauce-and-mirin reduction, wheat by default, and at 大黒家 the tempura is deliberately submerged in it rather than lightly brushed, so even the rice underneath is saturated. The few non-fried plates (sashimi, ぬた, 板わさ, 胡瓜もみ, くらげの酢の物) still come with wheat soy sauce or vinegar-miso dressings, the 板わさ is kamaboko (usually contains wheat starch), and the お吸物 and かき玉わん are undeclared dashi-and-soy soups. No allergen sheet, no gluten-free item, no wheat-free handling anywhere on the shop's site.
vegan_detail: The kitchen is prawn, kisu and kakiage; the batter is egg-bound wheat; the tare and the soups are bonito dashi; the fryer runs seafood all day. The only nominally plant plates are 胡瓜もみ, 茄子のしぎやき (miso-glazed aubergine, but a shigiyaki glaze normally carries dashi) and 楽京 / べったら漬け pickles. There is no vegan option and no separate fryer. A no.

roles: 四代目 — fourth-generation proprietor (unnamed on any published source)
chef_bio.origin: Denbōin-dōri, Asakusa — the same street the business has stood on since 1887
chef_bio.background: 大黒家 opened in 1887 (明治20年) on Denbōin-dōri, and it did not open as a tempura restaurant. It was a soba shop. The founder noticed that takings rose only on the days he sold tempura soba, and at the end of the Meiji era he closed the noodle business and became a tempura house outright, changing the shop sign from 大黒屋 to 大黒家 in the process. The shop tells this story itself, plainly, in its ごあいさつ page, and adds that the recipe has been held unchanged through to the current fourth-generation proprietor. What that recipe is comes down to two choices. First, the frying medium is pure sesame oil (ごま油だけを使って), which is what gives the batter its dark gold and its heavy fragrance — you smell it from the pavement while queueing. Second, the tare is deliberately thick and sharply salty-sweet, and the tempura is plunged into it rather than glazed, so the coating softens and fuses with the rice. This produces a 黒天丼 — a black tendon — that is the opposite of the modern light-and-crisp school, and visitors used to てんや-style tendon are routinely startled by it. The shop's own note about its people is characteristically unshowy: it says what pleases them most is that the head cook and the rest of the staff have worked there for many years and that customers are glad of it. The main shop seats about 200 across a detached traditional building with tatami rooms; a 別館 (annexe) a short walk away takes the overflow and also does banquet and memorial-service courses at ¥4,000–6,000.
chef_bio.philosophy: Do not change the taste. Sesame oil only, one dark tare, and a hundred-plus years of the same tendon.
chef_bio.specialty: 海老天丼 — four prawns overhanging the bowl, ¥2,700; the ¥2,300 mixed tendon (prawn, kisu, kakiage) is the sensible first order; 天麩羅定食 ¥2,900 serves the tempura undunked with tentsuyu and grated daikon for those who want to taste the batter itself.
anecdotes: The shop was a soba restaurant first and only became a tempura house because tempura soba outsold everything else — a business decision from around 1900 that produced a hundred-year Asakusa institution.
Locals' standard advice for a busy weekend is to skip the queue at the main shop and walk to the 別館 annexe, which serves the same tendon.
chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: tempura.co.jp/aisatsu.html carries the shop's own history: 明治二十年（1887）founding on 伝法院通り as a soba shop, the switch to tempura at the end of Meiji, the 大黒屋→大黒家 name change, the current 四代目 proprietor, the sesame-oil-only frying and the strong dark tare. tempura.co.jp/menu/index.html gives the full price list (天丼 ¥2,300 / ¥2,500, 海老天丼 ¥2,700, 天麩羅 ¥2,450 / ¥2,550, 海老天麩羅 ¥2,700, 天丼定食・天麩羅定食 ¥2,900, お吸物 ¥350, sashimi ¥2,400, annexe banquet courses ¥4,000–6,000) with tax included. Tabelog 13003696 gives 東京都台東区浅草1-38-10, 03-3844-1111, 11:00–20:00 daily, 200 seats, all-non-smoking, cash only (カード不可・電子マネー不可・QRコード決済不可), no parking, no reservations (予約不可), an オープン日 of 1887 and a ¥2,000–2,999 spend. No source anywhere mentions allergens, gluten or vegetarian options.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One shared sesame-oil kettle fries the entire menu in wheat batter, all day, for a 200-seat room. There is nothing to protect and no separate fryer.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature tare is a soy-sauce reduction and the tempura is submerged in it, soaking the rice below. The tentsuyu served with the teishoku is the same base. No gluten-free tamari is mentioned anywhere.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Prawn, kisu and mixed-seafood kakiage share the fryer continuously; the tare and both soups (お吸物, かき玉わん — the latter with egg) are dashi-based.

positives.text: The shop publishes its full menu with tax-inclusive prices online, so you can decide before joining the queue.
An English page exists on the official site, and the 天麩羅定食 serves the tempura dry with tsuyu on the side — the one order that lets you see what you are eating before it is sauced.

cultural_comfort.level: Easy to enter, hard to eat safely
cultural_comfort.note: As a room it is one of the most visitor-friendly doors in Asakusa: 200 seats in a detached traditional building on Denbōin-dōri, no reservation needed or possible, entirely non-smoking, children welcome, tatami as well as tables, an English page on the website, and open 11:00–20:00 every day. Two practical warnings. It is cash only — no cards, no IC money, no QR payment — which catches visitors out constantly. And the queue on weekends and festival days (Sanja Matsuri, the Hōzuki-ichi, Sensō-ji New Year) is long; the 別館 annexe two minutes away serves the same food with a shorter wait. For anyone avoiding gluten this is a look-don't-eat listing: it is a famous piece of Edo food history, and every single thing in it is wheat.

enrich_note: CONFIRMED. Tabelog 13003696 and the shop's own site (tempura.co.jp) agree on 東京都台東区浅草1-38-10 and 03-3844-1111; coordinates replaced with the Tabelog geo (35.712747, 139.795579). Full menu and prices taken directly from the shop's menu page. gf 'no' and vegan 'no' are structural, not an absence of evidence — the whole menu is wheat batter in one shared sesame-oil fryer, finished in a soy-sauce tare. Flagging for the app: cash only, no reservations.

name: 浅草 天ちゃ
cuisine: A six-seat standing-and-counter tempura bar two minutes behind Sensō-ji doing 天ぷら茶漬け — shiba-shrimp kakiage over rice with dashi poured through it — plus morning tendon sets from 8:30; luxury three-prawn tendon ¥2,400, most visits ¥1,000–2,000
neighborhood: Asakusa 2-chōme, two minutes on foot from Sensō-ji — 192 m from Asakusa Station on the Tsukuba Express (about 5 min), under 10 min from the Ginza / Toei Asakusa / Tobu Asakusa stations
hours_raw: 月・火・金・土・日 08:30 - 15:30（L.O. 料理15:00／ドリンク15:15）　水・木 定休　※朝メニューは8:30-10:00までオーダー可能（自社サイトは定休日を火・水と表記）
gf_detail: A tempura specialist: wheat batter, one fryer, all service. The signature 天ぷら茶漬け compounds it — the kakiage is fried in wheat batter and then a dashi broth is poured over it, and that broth is a soy-sauce-seasoned dashi (wheat by default in Japan) which the fried batter then absorbs. Breakfast sets add 豚汁, a miso soup whose miso is unspecified and may be barley. No allergen sheet, no gluten-free item, no wheat-free line anywhere on the shop's site or Tabelog page.
vegan_detail: Shiba shrimp, three kinds of prawn, Hokkaidō scallop, fried chicken and Iwanaka pork in the breakfast 豚汁 — the menu is animal from end to end, the ochazuke broth is bonito dashi, and the batter is egg-and-wheat. Tabelog also files the shop under 魚料理にこだわる. There is no vegan option and no separate fryer.

chef_bio.origin: Asakusa 2-chōme, Taitō-ku — a small unit two or three minutes' walk behind Sensō-ji
chef_bio.background: No name is published for the owner-cook, and no source names one, so none is invented here. The shop's identity is a historical argument rather than a personality. Its own site opens by pointing out that tempura in Edo was street food — sold from yatai, eaten standing, on skewers, dipped into a communal bowl of tsuyu — and that this is what it is trying to put back: a counter you stand or perch at, tempura fried in front of you and handed over immediately, and a tagline it repeats, 「熱々の天婦羅は音がする!!」, hot tempura makes a sound. The room holds six. The signature is 天ぷら茶漬け, a shiba-shrimp kakiage set over rice with a rich dashi poured through it so the batter half-dissolves; alongside it run a prawn tendon, a Hokkaidō scallop kakiage fried only to half-done so the centre stays rare, an egg tendon set with fried chicken, and a ¥2,400 luxury tendon built on three different prawns. Unusually for a tempura shop it opens at 8:30 and runs a dedicated breakfast menu until 10:00, with 豚汁 made from Iwanaka pork spare ribs — which, in a district where almost nothing serves a cooked breakfast, is most of the reason locals rate it. It closes at 15:30; there is no dinner service. Reservations are not taken at all, seating is strictly in arrival order, and in summer they run a 氷結そうめん where the frozen dashi is shaken to a shaved-ice texture at the counter in front of you.
chef_bio.philosophy: Tempura as Edo fast food — fried to order, eaten immediately at a counter of six, from breakfast onwards.
chef_bio.specialty: 天ぷら茶漬け with shiba-shrimp kakiage; morning tendon and 豚汁 sets from 8:30; half-rare Hokkaidō scallop kakiage; ¥2,400 three-prawn 贅沢海老天丼.
anecdotes: Opens at 8:30 with a proper breakfast menu, which in Asakusa — where most kitchens start at 11:00 — makes it one of very few places to get a hot cooked meal early.
chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: asakusatencha.com states the address 東京都台東区浅草２－７－２１, the 8:30–15:30 (L.O. 15:00) hours, the two-to-three-minute walk from Sensō-ji, the Edo-yatai concept and the 「熱々の天婦羅は音がする!!」 tagline, and lists the tempura-ochazuke signature, the shrimp tendon, the half-rare scallop kakiage, the egg tendon with fried chicken, the ¥2,400 luxury three-prawn tendon and the breakfast sets with Iwanaka-pork 豚汁. Tabelog 13299060 corroborates the address, gives 050-3503-7252, the 08:30–15:30 hours with Wednesday and Thursday closed, 6 seats, no reservations (来店順), all non-smoking, a ¥1,000–1,999 spend, cards and IC money and PayPay/WeChat accepted, multilingual menus in English, simplified Chinese and Korean, English-speaking staff, and a photo menu; a review there describes the summer 氷結そうめん being shaken at the counter. Note that the shop's own site and Tabelog disagree on which two days are the closing days. Neither source mentions allergens.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Single fryer, wheat batter, six seats — every item on the menu goes through the same oil. No separate fryer and no allergen statement.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The ochazuke broth poured over the kakiage is a seasoned dashi, and the tendon tare is a soy-sauce reduction; no gluten-free tamari is named. The breakfast 豚汁 uses unspecified miso, which may be barley-based.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Shrimp, scallop, chicken and pork all pass through the same six-seat kitchen; the ochazuke broth is bonito dashi and the batter contains egg.

positives.text: Menus in English, simplified Chinese and Korean, at least one English-speaking staff member, and a photo menu — unusually well set up for visitors given the size of the room.
You sit at the counter watching every piece being fried, so what is in your food is visible before you commit to it. Cards, IC money and QR payment all accepted.

cultural_comfort.note: Small but visitor-ready: six seats, all non-smoking, no dress code, multilingual and photo menus, English spoken, and every payment method including PayPay and WeChat Pay. No reservations are taken — you queue and are seated in arrival order — and with six seats that queue moves in fits, so go at 8:30 rather than at noon. It shuts at 15:30 and there is no dinner. The one thing to check before you walk over: the shop's own site says it closes Tuesday and Wednesday while Tabelog says Wednesday and Thursday, so confirm the day on their Instagram first. For a gluten-avoiding traveller this is not a stop — it is a wheat-batter specialist — but it is a genuinely good early-morning option for everyone else two minutes from Sensō-ji.

enrich_note: CONFIRMED, with a small name correction: the light record read 「浅草天ちゃ」 and the business writes itself 「浅草 天ちゃ」. Tabelog 13299060 and the shop's own site agree on 東京都台東区浅草2-7-21; coordinates replaced with the Tabelog geo (35.714833, 139.794419), moving the pin about 350 m north-east of the neighbourhood-centroid guess. Hours flagged irregular because the shop's site gives Tuesday/Wednesday as the closing days and Tabelog gives Wednesday/Thursday — that conflict is unresolved and a traveller should check Instagram before going. No chef name is published, so chef_bio.chef_name is left null. gf 'no' is structural (wheat batter, single fryer, soy-seasoned dashi poured over the batter), not an absence of evidence.

name: 三松寿司
cuisine: A 1958 Asakusa sushi house run by a mother and daughter, doing both Edomae nigiri and Osaka-style pressed sushi — the two things to order are hikarimono (kohada) and anago, and the battera, a kombu-wrapped pressed mackerel that has been on the counter since the shop opened; nigiri sets around ¥3,000–3,300, battera about ¥2,000, most visits ¥4,000–6,000
neighborhood: Asakusa 1-chōme, on the Kaminarimon side of the district away from the Nakamise crush — 298 m from Asakusa Station on the Tsukuba Express, about 7 min from the Ginza-line and Toei Asakusa-line Asakusa stations
gf_detail: No gluten-free claim and no allergen sheet — but sushi is one of the few Japanese cuisines where an informed celiac has something to work with, so the detail matters. The shari itself is rice, rice vinegar, sugar and salt, and this shop makes a point of its long-refined vinegar; plain raw nigiri is close to safe. What is not safe is everything painted on: Edomae nigiri is brushed with nikiri, a soy-sauce reduction, and the anago — one of the shop's two signatures — is finished with tsume, a thick soy-and-mirin glaze. Both are wheat by default and nothing here names a gluten-free tamari. The 玉子 is a dashimaki that normally contains mirin and soy, and the 梅しそ巻き in the set is fine but the accompanying soup is undeclared. The workable approach is to sit at the counter, ask for neta without nikiri, skip the anago and the tamago, and bring your own tamari — but that is a conversation in Japanese with a shop that has published nothing about allergens, so this stays at 'ask'.
vegan_detail: A sushi counter whose entire identity is silver-skinned fish and conger eel. There is no vegan set, no vegetable nigiri line advertised, and the soup is dashi. Nothing here to work with.

chef_bio.chef_name: 奥隅由規子 (Okusumi Yukiko) — second-generation itamae; with 奥隅美智子 (Okusumi Michiko), the ōkami
roles: 二代目 女性寿司職人 (second-generation woman sushi chef, at the counter since 2014)
大女将 (the founder's widow/mother, still working the room in her nineties)
chef_bio.origin: Asakusa 1-chōme, Taitō-ku — the shop has stood on the same spot since 1958
chef_bio.background: 三松寿司 opened in Asakusa in 1958 (昭和33年) and is still in the same family. The founding master stood behind the tsuke-dai for fifty-five years; when he stopped, his daughter took the counter rather than let the shop close, and she has been the itamae since 2014 — a woman running an Edomae counter, which is still rare enough in Tokyo to be the thing every write-up leads with. She is not doing it alone: the ōkami, her mother, is in her nineties and still in the room, greeting, pouring and prepping, and it is her shari — the vinegared rice, made with a vinegar blend the shop says it has refined over decades — that the daughter inherited and now makes. The shop's own line about itself is that it has kept two boards up for more than half a century: 江戸前 and 大阪寿司, Edo-style nigiri and Osaka-style pressed sushi, which is an unusual pairing for a Tokyo shop. Its self-declared 二枚看板 — the two names over the door — are 光りもの (the silver-skinned, vinegar-cured fish: kohada above all) and 穴子 (conger eel). The battera, kombu-topped pressed mackerel, has been made since the founding. Sixteen seats, mostly counter, with a small four-seat tatami; reservations taken; no cards.
chef_bio.philosophy: Keep the vinegar, keep the two boards — Edomae and Osaka pressed sushi — and keep the shop open by handing it down rather than selling it.
chef_bio.specialty: 小肌 and the rest of the hikarimono; 穴子; 鯖寿司（バッテラ）, the shop's dish since 1958; a full nigiri set with soup around ¥3,240.
anecdotes: The predecessor worked the counter for fifty-five years; his daughter took over in 2014 and became one of a small number of women running an Edomae sushi counter in Tokyo.
The ōkami, in her nineties, still works the floor — the shari recipe the daughter uses is her mother's.
chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own site (asakusa-mimatsu.com) states 浅草で昭和３３年（１９５８年）創業の江戸前寿司と大阪寿司の三松寿司, names its recommendations as 小肌・穴子・鯖寿司（バッテラ）, calls 光りもの and 穴子 its 二枚看板, and gives the phone 03-3841-5717 and an English page. おとなの週末Web (article 233317) names the proprietors 奥隅由規子さん and 奥隅美智子さん, dates the founding to about sixty years before its 2018 publication, records that the predecessor worked fifty-five years before his daughter took over, notes that the shari is the mother's, and lists a ¥3,240 special nigiri set (chūtoro, squid, akami, akagai, uni, tamago, ebi, anago, ume-shiso roll, soup), バッテラ at ¥1,940 and hikarimono at ¥210–480 a piece, with 16 counter seats and reservations accepted. Syupo (archives/99871) independently describes the 90-something 大女将 and the second-generation daughter behind the tsuke-dai, and prices the battera at ¥2,200 and a large Kenbishi at ¥1,500. That weekend lunch, in a mostly quiet part of Asakusa 1-chōme away from the Nakamise crowds, is the easiest way in. A woman running an Edomae counter with her ninety-something mother beside her is the kind of shop this app exists to find.

name: 麺屋 つけ麺 太輔
cuisine: Thick fish-and-pork-bone tsukemen behind Kaminarimon, open to 3 a.m. — the noodle was co-developed over some fifty or sixty meetings with Asakusa Kaikarō and is meant to be eaten plain first, like soba, before it goes near the dip; garlic, ebi and chilli-jan variants plus a mazemen, ¥1,000–2,000, cash only
neighborhood: Kaminarimon 1-chōme, a couple of streets back from the Kaminarimon gate — 244 m and about 3 min from Tawaramachi Station (Tokyo Metro Ginza line), roughly 8 min from Asakusa Station
gf_detail: This is a wheat shop that says so proudly. The whole concept is the noodle: a medium-thick wheat noodle developed jointly with 浅草開化楼, a long-established Tokyo noodle factory, over roughly fifty to sixty meetings starting from the choice of wheat, and the shop's own copy praises its 小麦の風味 — its wheat aroma — and asks you to eat it plain to taste it. The dip is a pork-bone-and-fish double soup; the mazemen is built on a soy-sauce tare; the ramen line includes 醤油 and 鴨醤油. Gyōza wrappers are wheat. There is no gluten-free item, no rice-noodle option, no allergen sheet, and one pot of boiling wheat-noodle water all service.
vegan_detail: Pork bone and fish in the base soup, six kinds of domestic prawn in the ebi tsukemen, chāshū and kakuni as standard toppings, back-fat in the mazemen, an egg option, and a heavily-used 魚粉 (dried-fish powder) shaker on the table. There is no vegetable or plant-based bowl anywhere on the menu.

roles: co-developer of the house noodle with 浅草開化楼
chef_bio.origin: Kaminarimon 1-chōme, Taitō-ku — a few minutes' walk from Tawaramachi Station on the Ginza line
chef_bio.background: No owner name is published on the shop's site, its Tabelog page or its social accounts, so none is given here. What the shop does document, at unusual length, is how the noodle was made. The owner writes that he had spent years chasing 'a good noodle' in a genre where being tasty is taken for granted, and that eating 浅草開化楼's noodles for the first time was a shock he never got over — 開化楼 being one of Japan's oldest and most-cited noodle makers, the supplier behind a long list of Tokyo's serious ramen shops. He went to them and they built a noodle together: roughly fifty to sixty meetings, starting from which wheat to use, ending in a formula the shop calls a trade secret. It began as an extremely thick noodle and was thinned — deliberately, with service time calculated — to a gauge that keeps a firm core inside a chewy body. The pitch that follows from that is the shop's whole argument: eat the noodle on its own first, the way a soba drinker eats soba plain, before dipping it. The dip is a straight-down-the-middle thick fish-and-tonkotsu, which the shop concedes is the most over-served style in Tokyo ('またおま系') and defends on the grounds that it is skimmed and cleaned constantly through the cook rather than left to go muddy. Round it sit variants: an ebi tsukemen using six kinds of domestic prawn including Ise-ebi; a garlic version using five kilos of coarsely-ground fresh garlic ground every morning; a 辛醬 version built on a dozen-plus pastes and spices including tōbanjan, tenmenjan and gochujang; a soy-tare mazemen with back fat; and a plain tonkotsu-gyokai ramen. On the counter sit four house condiments the shop names individually — a garlic vinegar, an addictive chilli powder blend, a deep-roasted fish powder, and the rest. The stated ambition is not modest: 「つけ麺は日本の文化になる」 — tsukemen will become Japanese culture — and to take it to the whole country.
chef_bio.philosophy: The noodle is the dish. Build it with the best maker you can find, then ask the customer to taste it naked before it meets the soup.
chef_bio.specialty: 濃厚魚介豚骨つけ麺; エビつけ麺 with six domestic prawns; ニンニクつけ麺; 辛醬つけ麺; 太輔流まぜめん. Toppings run to ajitama, chāshū and kakuni, with chāshū-don and a shibi-kara chāshū-don on the rice side.
anecdotes: The house noodle took around fifty to sixty development meetings with 浅草開化楼, beginning with the choice of wheat.
Five kilos of fresh garlic are coarsely ground every morning for the garlic tsukemen.
Open until 3 a.m. — one of the few serious noodle bowls available in Asakusa in the middle of the night.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork-bone and fish double soup, chāshū and kakuni toppings, back fat in the mazemen, prawn in the ebi bowl, and a fish-powder shaker on every table.

positives.text: The full menu with dish descriptions is published on the shop's own site, so you can see exactly what is in each bowl before going.
All-non-smoking, 26 seats, open 11:00 to 03:00 — genuinely useful late-night coverage in Asakusa.

cultural_comfort.level: Easy in practice, but a Japanese-only noodle bar
cultural_comfort.note: A straightforward walk-in: 26 seats, counter-led, all non-smoking, no reservations, no queue system to learn. Two things to know before you go. It is cash only — no cards and no IC money — and it closes on no fixed schedule (不定休), so check the shop's X or Instagram the day you plan to go. Nothing suggests English menus or English-speaking staff. The genuine draw for a late traveller is the 3 a.m. close. For anyone avoiding gluten this is a no-go, and not a marginal one: the shop's entire identity is a wheat noodle it spent a year developing.

cuisine: A thirteen-seat house-noodle shop a minute from Tawaramachi doing a modern Tokyo shōyu — high-hydration medium-thick noodles cut in-house, a katsuo-forward dashi carrying animal fat, ramen about ¥850 and the TRY-award tsukemen about ¥900, small rice ¥150; ¥1,000–2,000 a head

gf_detail: A self-milling, self-cutting wheat-noodle shop: the noodle is the point, it is made on the premises daily, and flour dust is in the air of a thirteen-seat room. The house style is 東京醤油 — the tare is soy sauce, wheat by default, and no gluten-free tamari is named. The dashi is bonito-forward with animal fat behind it. roles: TRY Ramen Awards 2024, new-shop tsukemen category — 2nd place
chef_bio.origin: Kotobuki 2-chōme, Taitō-ku — a corner unit of the World Mansion Tawaramachi building, one minute from Tawaramachi Station
chef_bio.background: The pedigree here is unusually well-documented for a thirteen-seat shop, because the TRY Ramen Awards profiled the owner directly. 神久保佑輔 trained first at 春木屋, the Ogikubo shop that is one of the founding names of Tokyo ramen and effectively defined the postwar 東京ラーメン idiom. He then entered the 地雷原 group, and it is there — the profile is explicit about this — that he built his noodle-making technique, 製麺技術, which is the thing his own shop is named for. He also trained in the 凪 group and worked alongside several very busy shops, and the profile sums him up as carrying 豊富な知識, a broad body of knowledge, rather than one house's dogma. What he does with it is deliberately unshowy: a Tokyo shōyu that reviewers describe as having no rough edges, a dashi built on katsuo with animal umami behind it, visible fat on the surface and just enough viscosity that it does not read as thin — a bowl written up as a 'shin-Tokyo ramen', the old idiom rebuilt rather than replaced. The noodles are cut in the shop, medium-thick, high hydration, slightly flattened, and the shop's argument is that this texture is simply not available from a supplier. In 2024 the tsukemen took second place in the new-shop tsukemen category of the TRY Ramen Awards, which is Tokyo's most-watched ramen ranking. Thirteen seats — five at the counter, eight at tables — no reservations, no takeaway, no delivery, no parking, and you pay after eating rather than at a ticket machine. A second shop, 自家製麺うるちⅡ, has since opened in Asakusabashi.
chef_bio.philosophy: Make the noodle yourself, because the texture you want cannot be bought; then build a Tokyo shōyu clean enough that the noodle is what you notice.
chef_bio.specialty: 東京醤油ラーメン (about ¥850); the TRY-awarded つけめん (about ¥900) with thick noodles, a rich dip and pork-arm chāshū; a 東京塩 version; small rice ¥150.
anecdotes: Trained at 春木屋 in Ogikubo — one of the shops usually credited with inventing the Tokyo ramen style he now serves.
Learned noodle-making inside the 地雷原 group, which is why the shop is named 自家製麺 — 'house-made noodles'.
Took 2nd place for tsukemen in the new-shop category of the 2024 TRY Ramen Awards, and has since opened a second shop in Asakusabashi.

Thirteen seats, all non-smoking, 65 m from the station, and reviewers report walking in without a wait outside peak hours.

neighborhood: Nishi-Asakusa 1-chōme — 88 m, one minute, from Tawaramachi Station exit 3 (Tokyo Metro Ginza line); 5 min from Asakusa Station exit A2 on the Tsukuba Express

gf_detail: Wheat noodles are the dish, so this is a no regardless of anything else — but the ingredient detail is worth recording because it is unusually well documented and one part of it is genuinely interesting. The shop makes its own 甜面醤 from 八丁味噌, and Hatchō miso is a pure soybean miso with no barley or wheat in it — a rarity. That does not rescue the bowl. The 豆板醤 is built on 四川豆板醤 and 郫県豆板醤; Pixian broad-bean paste conventionally contains wheat flour, and the shop does not say otherwise. The noodles are wheat. The Level-0 option removes the rāyu and huajiao but the shop explicitly warns that the minced pork still carries doubanjiang, so even the mildest bowl keeps the wheat-suspect paste. There is no allergen sheet and no gluten-free item.
vegan_detail: Pork mince (そぼろ) is in every bowl including the Level-0 one, the pāikō topping is fried pork cutlet, and there is a mābō-dōfu rice bowl that is standard minced-pork mapo. The extra-vegetable topping (mizuna, kaiware, ¥100) and the coriander are add-ons to a meat bowl, not a vegan route. No plant-based broth is offered.

roles: owner-operated two-shop Sichuan tantanmen house (湯島本店 opened first; 浅草 is the second shop, plus a Kitte Granché outlet)
chef_bio.origin: Yushima 3-chōme, Bunkyō-ku for the head shop; this record is the Nishi-Asakusa branch beside Tawaramachi Station
chef_bio.background: No chef name is published on the shop's site, its Tabelog pages or its social accounts, so none is asserted here. What the shop publishes instead is an unusually explicit statement of intent. 阿吽 — a-un — is the Sanskrit pair: 阿 the first sound made with the mouth open, 吽 the last made with it closed, together the beginning and end of all things. The shop maps them onto itself: 阿 is 本物, the real thing — 「安心、安全な食材」, safe and trustworthy ingredients, and a taste no one else can copy, pursued daily; 吽 is the wisdom and experience that turns into hospitality. It states plainly that its tantanmen is not a trend or an invention but something built on 食養生, food-as-health thinking. The technique is documented ingredient by ingredient. The rāyu is made in-house by slowly drawing flavour out of nine medicinal herbs and spices. The huajiao is used only from the outermost layer of the peppercorn, where the aroma is strongest, and is ground fresh every day so it does not fade. The tenmenjan is made in-house from Hatchō miso; the doubanjiang is made in-house from Sichuan and Pixian broad-bean pastes. The rice is contract-farmed terraced Koshihikari from Ukyō-ku in Kyoto, grown at 500 m on 800 stacked paddies with snowmelt water. The room plays jazz. Heat and numbness are ordered independently from 0 to 6 — Level 3 is the house standard, Level 2 is recommended for first-timers, Level 6 costs ¥100 extra and is served only to people who have already had Level 5, and is described as roughly ten times its heat. The Asakusa branch is eight counter seats and opens every day; the Yushima head shop is 17 seats and closes Tuesdays.
chef_bio.philosophy: 阿吽 — begin with real ingredients and end with real hospitality. Tantanmen as 食養生 rather than as a trend, with every paste, oil and grain made or sourced deliberately.
chef_bio.specialty: 白胡麻担担麺 and 黒胡麻担担麺 ¥1,200; the soupless (つゆ無し) versions of both at the same price; 担担つけ麺 ¥1,250; a half-size children's bowl ¥550; 麻婆豆腐丼 and 阿吽タコライス ¥400 each; toppings include pāikō ¥400, onsen egg ¥120 and coriander ¥150.
anecdotes: Heat (rāyu) and numbness (huajiao) are ordered as two separate 0–6 dials and can be mixed freely — rāyu 3 with huajiao 1, for instance.
Level 6 is sold only to customers who have already eaten Level 5, and the shop rates it at about ten times Level 5's heat.
The rice is terraced-paddy Koshihikari from a contract farm in Ukyō-ku, Kyoto, grown at 500 m on snowmelt water — an odd thing for a noodle shop to care about.

It gives the Asakusa branch as 東京都台東区西浅草1-1-13 カーサ田原町1F, 03-5828-5525, 平日 11:00–15:00 and 17:30–21:00, 土日祝 11:00–21:00, 定休日無休, 8 counter seats, all non-smoking. Tabelog 13178031 corroborates the address and phone, gives 88 m from Tawaramachi exit 3, 8 counter seats, no reservations, cash only, a ¥1,000–1,999 spend, and a 3.55 rating over 530 reviews, and notes the shop may close early when ingredients run out. Tabelog also lists sibling shops at 湯島本店 (13042564) and キッテグランシェ (13231656). No source mentions allergens or gluten.

gf_cross_contamination.text: One wheat-noodle pot in an eight-seat room, all service. No allergen policy is published.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house doubanjiang is built on Sichuan and Pixian broad-bean pastes; Pixian doubanjiang conventionally contains wheat flour and the shop does not state otherwise. It is present even in the Level-0 bowl, in the pork mince. Against that, the house tenmenjan is made from Hatchō miso, which is a soybean-only miso — the one wheat-free element in the seasoning.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork mince is in every bowl including Level 0; pāikō is fried pork; the mabo-dofu rice bowl is minced-pork mapo. Vegetable and coriander toppings are additions to a meat bowl.

positives.text: The 0-to-6 heat and numbness scale is published with a written description of each level, including a genuine Level 0 with no chilli oil and no Sichuan pepper — very unusual, and useful for anyone with a low chilli tolerance or a sensitive gut.

The shop publishes what its rāyu, tenmenjan, doubanjiang, huajiao and rice are actually made from — far more ingredient transparency than a typical noodle shop, which makes a dietary conversation possible even without an allergen sheet.
All non-smoking, children's half-portion on the menu, high chairs at the Yushima head shop.

cultural_comfort.note: Eight counter seats one minute from Tawaramachi Station, open every day of the year including weekends and holidays, all non-smoking, with a full price list published online in advance. Cash only, and no reservations — you queue. Because it is so small it can also close early if it runs out (材料なくなり次第閉店), so it is not a place to arrive at 20:45. The ordering has one genuinely traveller-friendly feature: you choose heat and numbness separately on a written 0–6 scale, so 'no chilli at all' is a normal order here rather than an awkward request. There is no English menu evidenced, but the numbers do most of the work. Not a stop for anyone avoiding gluten.

name: PANNINI 浅草
cuisine: The Asakusa outpost of PANNINI, the bakery arm of the Ginza Italian restaurant BERNINI — olive-oil-based Italian breads rather than butter ones, a porcini bread the group calls its own invention, house focaccia, truffle-egg sandwiches and bomboloni; opens at 7:00, 24 seats to eat in, cashless only, roughly ¥1,000–2,500
neighborhood: Kotobuki 4-chōme, on the Kappabashi side between Tawaramachi and Kuramae — 331 m from Tawaramachi Station (Tokyo Metro Ginza line)
gf_detail: A wheat bakery. The whole product line is Italian bread and dolce — focaccia, porcini bread, bolognese bread, sandwiches, bomboloni, panna cotta — baked on site, which means airborne flour throughout the room and shared boards, ovens and slicers. No gluten-free line, no allergen sheet and no wheat-free product is mentioned by the group, the Ginza shop's coverage, or the Asakusa listing. The one thing worth knowing is that the breads are built on olive oil rather than butter, which the group states plainly; that is a dairy point, not a gluten one.
vegan_detail: Genuinely unresolved, so it is left at 'ask' rather than guessed either way. The group's own line is that the breads are olive-oil-based and deliberately light — 「オリーブオイルをベースにヘルシーで軽やかな食感のパンたち」 — and a plain olive-oil focaccia is frequently vegan by construction. But nothing is declared: the published items that can be checked are mostly not vegan (bolognese bread, bolognese cheese bread, caprese and chicken focaccia, truffle-egg sandwich, bomboloni, panna cotta), and no source states whether the plain breads contain milk, egg or honey. Ask at the counter about the plain focaccia and the porcini bread specifically.

roles: bakery brand of the BERNINI Restaurant Group; the breads and dolce are made by the chef of BERNINI GINZA
chef_bio.origin: Ginza — PANNINI began as the bread-and-dolce spinoff of BERNINI GINZA, an Italian restaurant of around twenty years' standing; this record is its Asakusa shop in Kotobuki 4-chōme
chef_bio.background: PANNINI is not a neighbourhood bakery that happens to be Italian; it is an Italian restaurant's bread programme let out of the kitchen. The BERNINI group describes it in one line — 「BERNINI GINZAのシェフが織りなすイタリア料理パンとドルチェ」, Italian-cuisine bread and dolce woven by the chef of BERNINI GINZA — and the defining technical choice is that the breads are built on olive oil rather than butter, aiming at a light rather than a rich crumb. The house items it names are a porcini bread it says has no equivalent anywhere, its own focaccia, and bomboloni, the Italian filled doughnut. The Ginza shop opens at 7:30 and sells out through the afternoon; published prices there run from about ¥248 for a bomboloni to ¥324 for the bolognese bread, ¥410 for the bolognese-cheese and for focaccia, and up to about ¥594 for the porcini sandwiches, with a ¥1,200–1,500 brunch set added in 2024. The Asakusa shop opened on 3 December, keeps a longer day (7:00 to 19:00) and, unusually for a bakery, has 24 seats to sit and eat in. It arrived with some momentum: the brand's Italian doughnuts had been sold inside the Italy pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka-Kansai and were picked up by Japanese daytime television, and the Asakusa opening was covered on that basis. Treat that last strand as press context rather than as a claim about the shop's cooking.
chef_bio.philosophy: Restaurant-kitchen Italian baking: olive oil instead of butter, a light crumb, and savoury breads treated as dishes.
chef_bio.specialty: ポルチーニパン (porcini bread); house focaccia; トリュフたまごサンド (truffle-egg sandwich); ボロネーゼパン; ボンボローニ; panna cotta.
anecdotes: The brand's Italian doughnuts were sold in the Italy pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka-Kansai, which is how most Japanese coverage of the Asakusa opening frames it.
It opens at 07:00 — earlier than almost anything else in the Tawaramachi–Kuramae stretch — and has 24 seats, so it works as a sit-down breakfast rather than only a takeaway counter.

Tabelog 13316955 gives the Asakusa shop as 東京都台東区寿4-13-11, 03-6802-7377, 07:00–19:00, 24 seats, all non-smoking, reservations accepted, 331 m from Tawaramachi, and states 「現金はご利用いただけません」 — cards, transport IC, iD, QUICPay and PayPay only. An Instagram announcement surfaced via Yahoo Japan reads 「パンニーニ浅草、12/3からオープンいたしました」. No source mentions allergens, gluten-free or vegan items.

gf_cross_contamination.text: An on-site wheat bakery: flour in the air, shared ovens, boards and slicers, and open display of unwrapped bread. Nothing is protected from wheat here.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Cheese, egg, cured meat and bolognese sauce are all in the published product line and handled on the same counter; no separate preparation is described.

positives.text: The breads are built on olive oil rather than butter — the group states this itself — which is a real, if narrow, help for anyone avoiding dairy in the bread base.
24 seats, all non-smoking, open from 07:00, and fully cashless (cards, transport IC, iD, QUICPay, PayPay) — one of the easiest doors in the area for a visitor without yen.

cultural_comfort.note: About as low-friction as Tokyo gets: a bakery counter where you point at what you want, 24 seats to sit down in, all non-smoking, open from 07:00 to 19:00, reservations accepted, and the group's own website carries English. One practical warning that catches people out in the opposite of the usual direction — this shop does not take cash at all (「現金はご利用いただけません」). Bring a card or a phone. As at the Ginza shop, popular items sell through during the day, so early is better. Useless for a celiac; very good for an early breakfast if you are not avoiding wheat.

roles: owner-chef, from Sendai (no name published by any source)
chef_bio.origin: Sendai, Miyagi — the owner's home city, which the shop is entirely built around; the premises are in Matsugaya 1-chōme, Taitō-ku, behind Kappabashi
chef_bio.background: 杜都 is 杜の都, the city of trees — Sendai's own nickname — and that is the whole proposition: 旬菜, seasonal produce, from Sendai, in Tokyo. The owner is from Sendai and the shop's line about itself is 「仙台から直送した旬の食材を楽しむことができる和食系のお店です」, a Japanese restaurant where you can eat seasonal ingredients shipped straight up from Sendai. In practice that meant a menu that changed hard with the calendar: mountain vegetables and sansai in spring, and from November to March the dish it was best known for, せり鍋 — Sendai's water-dropwort hot pot, made in the Miyagi way with the roots left on and eaten for their crunch, in a duck-and-chicken broth, ¥2,400. Alongside it ran the city's other export, thick-cut 仙台牛タン grilled with miso at ¥2,500, a seven-variety sashimi plate at ¥2,200, charcoal-grilled 縞ほっけ at ¥1,100 and a warm potato salad at ¥850, with a Miyagi sake list including 日高見 and 乾坤一. It was small and adult and quiet — a few counter seats and three tables, eighteen covers in total, run for regulars — and it was step-free, listed as wheelchair-accessible, which is rare for an izakaya of this size. It opened on 25 May 2020, into the first months of the pandemic, and it is closing at the end of August 2026, a little over six years later. No owner name appears on Tabelog, on the aggregators, or in the two Japanese blog write-ups found.
chef_bio.philosophy: One prefecture's produce, sent up fresh and cooked plainly, with that prefecture's sake beside it.
chef_bio.specialty: せり鍋 (November–March) ¥2,400; 厚切り仙台牛タン ¥2,500; 刺身七種盛り ¥2,200; 縞ほっけ炭火焼き ¥1,100; 温かいポテトサラダ ¥850.
anecdotes: Opened 25 May 2020, in the first wave of the pandemic, and lasted just over six years.
The seri-nabe was served the Miyagi way — roots and all — which is the detail Sendai people check for and Tokyo shops usually skip.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No allergen policy published, and the shop is closing, so none can now be obtained. A shared charcoal grill and a single small kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The signature gyūtan is miso-grilled (miso is wheat- or barley-fermented unless stated to be a soybean-only type) and the seri-nabe broth and sashimi service both use ordinary soy sauce. No gluten-free tamari is named.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Duck-and-chicken nabe broth, beef tongue, sashimi and grilled fish; the seasonal vegetables are cooked within that menu, not apart from it.

positives.text: Listed as wheelchair-accessible (車椅子で入店可) and entirely non-smoking — unusual for an eighteen-seat izakaya.
